Anthropic says in its amended S-1 that its internal estimates and expectations about FUTURE models indicate that it may "imminently" meet the definition if "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI".

Under the RSP, this means that Anthropic observes or expects 2x the rate of progress in AI capabilities vs. the rate Anthropic would expect and the fastest rate of extended progress observed over at least 3 model generations without significant AI contributions to AI R&D, plus it's plausible that this doubling is due to automation of research and/or engineering such that it's likely that there will be even greater acceleration.

Note that "2x the rate of progress" means that 2 years of progress would be compressed into 1 year.  So, if Anthropic would have improved its models 9x in one year without AI-enabled acceleration, this threshold would be reached when Anthropic expects to be able to improve its models by 81x in one year (9^2).

What he actually did:

→ Claude Code desktop, Opus 5.5 on Medium effort. He says he only talked to Claude and had it do everything.
→ His manual work was 3 browser chores: a Google Cloud API key, a VPS, a domain.
→ Then one instruction: "update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize." Claude did it.
→ No login. Thumbnails are a frame from the middle of the video, not the A/B-tested face.
→ He shared the data as one zip: "point your Claude at it and ask for your own version."

YouTube has thousands of engineers on that feed. Karpathy had Medium effort.

The part people will miss is the signal he picked. YouTube ranks what keeps you watching tonight. HN comments show what people still vouch for years later. Same videos, different question.

And the hard part of the prompt is one distinction: recommended vs. mentioned. "Watch this talk" is a vote. "That talk was wrong" is a mention. Get that wrong and your feed fills with drama.

The prompt to build your own:

"You have a dataset of [comments / bookmarks / newsletters].
Goal: find the [videos / books / tools] people recommend to each other.
Step 1: Label 30 random items as RECOMMEND, MENTION or CRITICIZE. Show me the labels and stop.
Step 2: After I approve, run it on everything. Rank by distinct people recommending each item and how many years they kept doing it. Drop single-recommendation items and one-week spikes.
Step 3: Show the top 20 with your reasoning before building anything.
Step 4: Build one local page: grid, filters by topic and length, no login, likes saved in the browser."

Step 1 is what most people skip. 30 labels now saves you from 6,000 wrong ones later.

text:
I've seen a lot of debate on Shaun's SpaceX ($SPCX) model,so here's my two cents.

First, credit where due. His 2020 Starlink model, built when Starlink had zero revenue, had it at a ~$23bn run-rate by end-2025. It's at ~$20bn now. That's a remarkable call. And the wood-for-the-trees camp is right that taxes and working capital are noise. Novel businesses need first-principles forecasting, not extrapolation.

But here's the irony. Terrestrial compute is $569bn of his $731bn 2028 revenue (~78%). That's the least futuristic thing SpaceX does: renting GPUs in data centres on Earth. And unlike Starship or orbital compute, it has observable market prices.

So let's engage on his terms. He says compute is a commodity, SpaceX is the low-cost producer, and rev/GW and capex/GW move together.

In a commodity, the low-cost producer wins on cost, not price. And if scarcity reprices the whole market to $40bn/GW, Oracle earns it too on $37bn of capex. That's a boom for everyone, not distress that SpaceX can buy cheaply.

His 2028: $40bn revenue per GW, $30bn capex per GW
Oracle (Investor Day): $16bn revenue, $37bn capex
CoreWeave (reported): ~$7bn annualised revenue per active GW

So SpaceX is modelled as the low-cost producer AND charging 2.5x Oracle's price.

The coupling doesn't fix it. At Oracle's $16bn price, his ratio implies ~$12bn of capex per GW. Nvidia says its own share alone is ~$25bn/GW on Blackwell and ~$40bn on Rubin.

And his own 2026 numbers show capex of $40-55bn per GW, so the cost advantage is still a forecast.

Starship is an extraordinary moat in launch. It doesn't help sell compute in a Texas data centre at 2.5x market.

Genuine question: if compute is oil, why does SpaceX get 2.5x the oil price?

All good questions a few comments. Writing this quickly so not exactly addressing everything you asked:

1) I feel strongly that SpaceX is the low-cost producer for compute (initially terrestrial which becomes orbital)

2) BUT the analogy to oil breaks down in some important ways, mainly the lifetime of a "well" = "datacenter" is much shorter. This means being able to turn on new wells in a supply crunch is particularly valuable

I believe SpaceX will be able to turn on new datacenters 2-3 years faster than its competitors

3) With this point in mind, I'd forecast rev/GW goes down dramatically over the next 5 years. Back down to something like $10B/GW

I'd also forecast the CapEx/GW goes down dramatically over a similar time frame (likely 5 years definitely 10 years)

On the CapEx side, I believe SpaceX will benefit in the short term from some of the neoclouds (and maybe even hyperscalers) failing to turn on datacenters as quickly as they modeled which will force them to sell hardware at a discount to SpaceX

4) over the long term (5-10 years) I think CapEx/GW goes down dramatically as new fabs and also new technologies come online

People forget that four years ago nobody cared about chips or the AI build out (except for weirdos like me). It's about a 10 year delay from the time semis become the bottleneck before their supply chain is materially impacted

解决的问题：当前Agent受单会话隔离、人工切换、人类注意力瓶颈限制，无法支持多任务并行与始终在线工作。
